summary.title: Machine learning force field ranking of candidate solid electrolyte interphase structures in Li-ion batteries
summary.authors: James M Stevenson; Garvit Agarwal; Leif D Jacobson
summary.executive_summary:
This study addresses the critical gap in understanding the Solid-Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) in lithium-ion batteries, a complex passivating layer that remains poorly characterized due to the limitations of existing simulation methods. Traditional Density Functional Theory (DFT) methods are too slow for the necessary length and time scales, while classical force fields lack the accuracy for complex redox reactions. The authors propose a novel approach using a multitask machine learning force field (MLFF) based on the QRNN architecture to simulate SEI formation and rank candidate structures by predicted energy.

The methodology involves a combination of classical sampling and active learning. Initial SEI candidate structures were generated using the Schrödinger SEI Simulator with OPLS4 molecular dynamics, starting with 1 M LiPF6 in ethylene carbonate (EC). These candidates were then annealed using a reactive QRNN model under extreme conditions (400 K, 1000 atm) to ensure stability and reaction completion. The model was trained on a diverse dataset including periodic and non-periodic systems, labeled with PBE-D3 and wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD levels of theory, as well as a supplemental SPICE dataset for general organic chemistry to shape the latent space.

Key results demonstrate that the MLFF can stably simulate complex redox reactions, producing the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by energy. Statistical analysis of the bonding in these structures reveals that P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable configurations, while C-O and Li-F bonds correlate with less stability. The study validates the model against surface reaction energy barriers, showing reasonable accuracy. The authors conclude that this approach provides a quantitative foundation for understanding SEI chemistry and suggests future work on comparing multiple electrolyte formulations and applying other MLFF architectures like Nequip and MACE. This work represents a significant step toward using machine learning to model complex battery interphases, offering a pathway to optimize SEI composition for next-generation batteries.

judge_context:
Executive Summary

These candidates were then annealed using a reactive QRNN model under extreme conditions (400 K, 1000 atm) to ensure stability and reaction completion. The model was trained on a diverse dataset including periodic and non-periodic systems, labeled with PBE-D3 and wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD levels of theory, as well as a supplemental SPICE dataset for general organic chemistry to shape the latent space.

Key results demonstrate that the MLFF can stably simulate complex redox reactions, producing the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by energy. Statistical analysis of the bonding in these structures reveals that P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable configurations, while C-O and Li-F bonds correlate with less stability. The study validates the model against surface reaction energy barriers, showing reasonable accuracy. The authors conclude that this approach provides a quantitative foundation for understanding SEI chemistry and suggests future work on comparing multiple electrolyte formulations and applying other MLFF architectures like Nequip and MACE. This work represents a significant step toward using machine learning to model complex battery interphases, offering a pathway to optimize SEI composition for next-generation batteries.

Research Context
The Solid-Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) is a vital but poorly-understood material class in lithium-ion batteries. Key questions about SEIs, such as their amorphous or crystalline nature, remain unanswered. Existing pure density functionals underestimate reaction barriers and are too slow for SEI scales. Hybrid functionals struggle with metals and have poor computational scaling for periodic systems. Machine learning force fields (MLFFs) promise DFT accuracy with classical force field speed. Previous MLFFs have predicted properties of Li metal and organic liquids but not SEI interactions. Traditional force fields are difficult to fit for complex systems like the SEI.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to simulate and rank SEI candidate structures using machine learning. The hypothesis is that a multitask MLFF can model complex SEI reactions with sufficient accuracy. The study aims to produce the first set of SEI structures ranked by predicted energy. It is hypothesized that specific bond types correlate with the energetic stability of SEI structures. The authors predict that MLFFs can bridge the gap between DFT accuracy and classical speed. The goal is to enable future machine learning applications and comparison with experimental results.

Methodological Details
The reference level of theory for non-periodic systems is wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD. The reference level of theory for periodic systems is PBE-D3 in a plane wave basis. The study uses multiple rounds of active learning for data generation. Enhanced reaction sampling uses Artificial Force Induced Reactions (AFIR) and Nudged Elastic Band (NEB). A supplemental dataset of general organic chemistry, SPICE, was added to shape the latent space. The SPICE subset consists of elements H, Li, C, O, F, and P. The hidden layers of the neural networks were doubled to increase model capacity. Initial SEI candidates were generated using the Schrödinger SEI Simulator with OPLS4 MD. Each system starts with 700 molecules of EC and 52 ions each of Li+ and PF6-. The total number of atoms in each initial system is 7416. Four sets of candidates were defined with 5, 12, 23, and 33 added Li+ ions. Lithium oxide, carbonate, fluoride, and hydroxide were added to the training set. Non-equilibrium geometries were sampled by adding Gaussian noise to Cartesian coordinates. Periodic DFT was performed using Quantum Espresso with PBE functional and D3 correction. Gas-phase DFT was performed using Psi4 v1.6 with wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD.

Procedures And Architectures
The model architecture is a multitask QRNN with four output levels of theory. The loss function includes energy, force, and charge mean squared error. The Adamax optimizer with decoupled weight decay was used for training. The final model used a learning rate of 2e-3. Hidden layers of size 256, 224, and 192 were used for all elements. The batch size was set to 64. A weight decay of 1e-3 was used for the final model. The final model is an exponential moving average of training parameters. Initial liquid geometries were equilibrated using NPT ensemble for 1 ns. Solid-liquid interfaces started from a BCC lattice of lithium with optimized lattice constant. Candidates were annealed using reactive QRNN MD at 400 K and 1000 atm for 100 ps. Structures were ranked by mean potential energy over a 20 ps MD trajectory at 300 K. Lewis structures were recalculated using Schrödinger Materials Science Suite for bond analysis.

Key Results
The QRNN models gave stable dynamics despite extreme conditions applied during annealing. The study produced the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy. P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable structures. C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable structures. Adding SPICE data resulted in only an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE. The model was validated against surface reaction energy barriers. The lowest-energy SEI candidate from the 33 added Li subgroup was identified as the best. The model does not have enough capacity to overfit, so early stopping had little effect.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results suggest that specific bond types determine the energetic stability of SEI structures. Multitask training allows the model to handle diverse chemical systems without heavy capacity cost. The latent space of MLFF models contains unused capacity for broadening chemical applicability. This work provides a quantitative foundation for understanding lithium-ion battery interphases. The approach enables the ranking of candidate SEI structures for future optimization. The study demonstrates the feasibility of simulating complex redox reactive systems with MLFFs.

Contradictions And Limitations
The difficulty of characterizing the SEI experimentally is an obstacle to validation. Experimental values for density, diffusivity, viscosity, or elastic modulus do not exist for SEI. The model is not final, as its scope is still small compared to requirements. The study only used a single formulation of electrolyte, 1M LiPF6 in EC. The probability of being proven wrong by future events is high. The model was not trained on DFT-generated MD, AFIR, or NEB geometries to avoid test set leakage.

Claims
Multitask training with QRNN allows accurate simulation of complex SEI reactions. The model stably simulated extreme conditions and complex redox reactions. The model produced ranked SEI structures with reasonable energy predictions. The model's scope is limited and not yet final. This enables quantitative understanding of SEI chemistry.
Specific bond types correlate with SEI structural stability. P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable structures. C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable structures. The correlation is based on predicted energies, not experimental validation. This guides the design of more stable SEI formulations.

Data And Code Availability
The list of SEI candidate structures and energies is available on Figshare. Plotting scripts and initial solution structures are also provided in the repository.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Adding SPICE data did not significantly increase PBE-head validation RMSE. Higher weight decay reduced reaction barrier heights, so a conventional value was used. The model was validated against surface reaction energy barriers.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 4 shows bond counts with respect to total system energy for the most lithiated SEI set. Table 1 validates the model against surface reaction energy barriers.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first MLFF-based ranking of SEI candidate structures. 2. The strongest evidence is the stable simulation of complex redox reactions and bond stability correlations. 3. The future path involves comparing multiple electrolyte formulations and applying other MLFF architectures.
